strengths: Addresses an important question: why distributional RL can outperform expectation-based methods. The decomposition into a mean-bin loss and a residual-distribution loss provides a potentially useful interpretive perspective under its admissibility conditions.

Experiments cover eight Atari games and several continuous-control tasks, with three or five seeds, interpolation-weight sensitivity, and policy-entropy ablations. The observed task-dependent interactions between distributional critics and policy entropy merit further investigation.

The paper discusses relevant C51, fitted Q-iteration, and SAC literature, supplies appendix proofs and implementation details, and explicitly acknowledges the limitations of extending its categorical analysis to other distributional methods.
weaknesses: The central explanatory link is not established. Equation 4 decomposes a critic-fitting loss, whereas Equations 7–9 introduce an augmented-reward control objective. The paper does not show that ordinary categorical distributional RL optimizes this new objective. Proposition 4.3 concerns ideal minimizers as bin width vanishes; it does not establish equivalent neural-network updates or an exploration advantage.

The derivation of DERAC's objective contains a substantive mathematical error. In Appendix I, writing δ = T^πQθ* − Qθ, expanding the squared augmented residual requires the cross term 2√τ E[δ√H]. Equation 36 instead writes E[δH] and then discards it. No stated assumption makes this term vanish for arbitrary learned critics and target networks. Consequently, Equation 10 is not established as equivalent to the proposed Bellman-residual objective.

The convergence argument in Appendix H treats the entropy bonus as unchanged during policy improvement, although the target return distribution depends on the policy and the estimated distribution changes during learning. Boundedness alone does not justify this substitution. The proof supports policy iteration with a fixed external bonus, rather than the claimed coupled distribution-learning procedure.

Cross-entropy does not isolate distribution mismatch: H(μ,q) = H(μ) + KL(μ||q), so it can remain large even when q = μ. This undermines the specific interpretation that large bonuses identify poorly estimated returns. Intrinsic return randomness and reducible estimation uncertainty need to be distinguished.

The experiments report returns without directly measuring exploration, visitation coverage, or uncertainty reduction. Changing the target distribution in the ε ablation, or replacing a scalar critic with a distributional critic, also changes optimization and representation. These comparisons therefore cannot identify the proposed exploration mechanism. Interpolating performance between baselines likewise does not validate the tabular convergence theorem.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameters: the exact ε-to-ϵ transformation and probability-redistribution procedure are insufficiently specified, categorical support bounds and Atari-specific settings are missing, and plotted uncertainty bands are not clearly defined. These omissions matter because the target manipulation is central to the empirical argument.
